summary: 1933 steel lookout near Toano, first built for Chesapeake Pulp and Paper; now privately owned, with most of its boards missing according to the Register.

facts.design: 100-foot Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with a glass-enclosed cab
facts.status_note: Standing, but the Register says most of its boards are missing.

access.note: The Register lists a private owner and describes no public access.

events.note: Daily Press report of October 17, 1933 says a look-out was erected for Chesapeake Pulp and Paper Co. on H. P. Hazelwood's land; the Register also gives 1933
Federal survey station description: owned by the Chesapeake Corporation and operated in cooperation with the state Forest Service

evidence.quote: This 100-foot tall Aermotor LS-40 Tower that was built in 1933
a majority of the boards are missing

evidence.supports: cab still keeps most of its glass panels
evidence.quote: the cab seems to have a majority of its glass panels still in there

evidence.supports: a stand at the spot meant for the Osborne fire finder remains
evidence.quote: the stand for where the Osborne fire finder would have been

notes_for_editor: Height conflict: the 1933 Daily Press item (quoted on the Forest Lookouts page) says 120 feet; the 1942 NGS station description and the Register say about or exactly 100 feet. facts uses 30.5 m (100 ft). Owner conflict: the 1933 and 1942 sources name Chesapeake (Pulp and Paper Co., then Corporation); the Register names David Nice. No source read dates the change or explains the name change. facts.access level 'private' is inferred from the Register's private-owner line; no source describes public access or climbing. One WebSearch on the tower, Chesapeake and David Nice found nothing that ties them to this tower. The Register description is undated, so current condition is not verified. The Forest Lookouts page also gives a 1942 NGS designation (PID GV4691), which is not in the story.
